newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila's Reynolds hurt by import tariff cut.
newsitem.headline: Manila's Reynolds hurt by import tariff cut.

text.p: Reynolds Philippines Corp, one of the country's biggest manufacturers of aluminium products, said on Monday a tariff cut on imported aluminium was hurting its business.
"We are affected," Herman Vargas, vice president for marketing at Reynolds told Reuters.
The government cut tariffs on imported aluminium foil, plates, sheets, strips and coils to 10 percent at the start of the year from the previous 20 percent.

"As early as the last quarter of 1996, Reynolds already suffered a substantial decrease in volume sales brought about by the anticipated reduction in the tariff for 1997," president Jaime Gonzales said in a letter to the Philippine Board of Investments.
Reynolds officials said buyers of aluminium products began holding back orders in the fourth quarter last year in anticipation of the drop. Some opted to import their requirements.
The firm had to reduce the prices of its aluminium products by 10 percent to reflect the tariff cut, Vargas said.
Reynolds is the Philippines' sole manufacturer of aluminium sheets and foils. It is also one of the country's largest manufacturers of aluminium products used in construction.
The firm imported 12,000 tonnes of aluminium from Australia and the Middle East last year compared with 10,000 tonnes in 1995.
All Asia Securities Corp earlier forecast Reynolds would post a net income of 301 million pesos ($11.4 million) this year from 107 million pesos last year.
Reynolds reported a net income of 33.09 million pesos in the first quarter of 1997.
"Reynolds had a disappointing first quarter income largely due to higher interest charges on its loans," said All Asia Securities analyst Melvin Sico.
"But I expect interest charges to taper off for the rest of the year as it pays its loans from proceeds of its initial public offering," said Sico. The company went public in February.
Sico said All Asia was standing by its forecast "for the moment".
"The first quarter is usually a slow quarter," he said, adding All Asia was waiting for the release of second quarter earnings data to see if it was necessary to adjust the forecast.
"Reynolds now finds itself not only threatened but seriously prejudiced by a reduction in tariff duty that adversely affects its business operations and continued viability," Gonzales said.
Gonzales said Reynolds was opposed to the new tariff because semi-processed aluminium products were assessed the same, and in some cases even at a lower rate than raw materials.
Reynolds said the tariff should be maintained at 20 percent to correct the distortion.
"Reynolds needs adequate time to cope with the changing economic conditions," Gonzales said.
